entry: Involuntary termination of an employee's job for business reasons, usually as a cost-cutting measure. Originally, *layoff* meant a temporary interruption in work and pay; it now usually means the permanent elimination of a position, so *temporary layoff* is used for the older sense. Other [[Euphemism|euphemisms]] for permanent layoffs include downsizing, rightsizing and reduction in force (RIF). Downsizing became popular in companies during the 1980s and early 1990s as a way to cut costs and deliver better shareholder value. The U.S. Department of Labor defines a mass layoff as 50 or more workers laid off from the same company around the same time. Layoffs imply economic forces beyond anyone's control, while firings imply misconduct or failure. A study of 391 downsizing announcements by S&P 100 firms from 1990 to 2006 found that stock prices rose after layoff announcements, by more at firms that had laid off workers before.

Region of central Italy containing Rome, the national capital. Lazio, also called *Latium*, has 5,709,444 inhabitants and a GDP of more than €212 billion per year, making it Italy's second most populous region and second-largest economy after Lombardy. It was home to the [[Etruscan civilization|Etruscans]] and later the center of the [[Roman Republic]], the [[Roman Empire]], the [[Papal States]] and the Kingdom of Italy. Great artists lived and worked in Rome, especially during the Italian Renaissance. After World War II, the region grew rapidly, and today its economy centers on services, public administration, international trade and [[Tourism|tourism]].

American [[Basketball|basketball]] forward, nicknamed King James. He plays for the Philadelphia 76ers of the [[National Basketball Association|NBA]], having joined them in 2026, and he is the league's all-time leading scorer. The [[Cleveland]] Cavaliers made him the first overall pick in the 2003 draft, straight out of high school. He won four NBA championships with the Cavaliers, the [[Miami]] Heat and the [[Los Angeles Lakers]], and became the first player named Finals MVP with three different teams. James has won four NBA MVP awards and has been selected for the All-Star roster a record 22 times. He also won three Olympic gold medals with the U.S. national team. [[Forbes]] listed him among the world's ten highest-paid athletes 15 times.

American actor, director and television host. He played Geordi La Forge in [[Star Trek: The Next Generation]] (1987–1994) and Kunta Kinte in the ABC miniseries *Roots* (1977). He hosted the [[PBS]] children's series *Reading Rainbow* for 23 years (1983–2006), earning Daytime Emmy Awards and a Peabody Award as host and executive producer. He won a [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] for narrating *The Autobiography of Martin Luther King Jr.* and received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1990. From 2017 to 2024 he hosted the podcast *LeVar Burton Reads*, and since October 2024 he has hosted the game show *Trivial Pursuit* on [[The CW]].

Swiss-French architect and urban planner, regarded as a pioneer of modern architecture. Born in Switzerland as Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, he acquired French nationality in 1930. He designed buildings in Europe, Japan, India and the Americas, and was a founding member of the *Congrès International d'Architecture Moderne* (CIAM). He prepared the master plan for [[Chandigarh]], India, and designed several of its government buildings. In 2016, 17 of his projects in seven countries were inscribed as a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]]. He also designed furniture such as the LC4 chaise longue. His ties to [[Fascism|fascism]], [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]], [[Eugenics|eugenics]] and [[Benito Mussolini]] remain contested, and critics argue that some of his urban planning ideas were indifferent to existing cultural sites and social equality.

French daily newspaper founded in 1944. Hubert Beuve-Méry founded it, and [[Charles de Gaulle|General de Gaulle]] was a driving force behind its creation. It succeeded *Le Temps*, which had been shut down in 1944. Le Monde is the most widely read paid national daily in France, with 2.44 million readers in 2021, and it has around 500,000 subscribers. It describes itself as a "newspaper of record." Published in Paris, it appears in the early afternoon with the following day's date. A 2010 academic study characterized its editorial stance as center-left, and an April 2022 Ifop survey found that 48% of regular readers voted for left-wing candidates in the first round of the 2012 presidential election.

City (pop., 2020: 1,579,803) in Guanajuato state, [[Mexico]]. León is the most populous city and seat of its municipality, located in the Bajío region of the Mexican Plateau. Its [[Leather|leather]] industry makes shoes, boots, belts and jackets for national and international markets. Workers whose bodies were tinted green by treating leather gave the city's inhabitants the nickname *panzaverde* ("green belly"). Spanish colonial authorities founded the village in 1576. The [[Jesuits]] arrived in 1731 and were expelled from Mexico in 1767. León is considered one of Mexico's most environmentally friendly cities, with many cyclists and bike lanes integrated into its SIT transit system. In 2012 it received a "City Water Champion" award for sanitation, wastewater reuse and biogas cogeneration.

Chemical element with atomic number 82 and symbol Pb. Lead is a dense, soft, malleable metal with a low melting point that tarnishes to dull gray in air. Its principal ore, [[Galena]], often bears silver, and interest in silver led to widespread lead use in [[Ancient Rome|ancient Rome]]. Production did not reach comparable levels again until the [[Industrial Revolution]]. Lead alloys could be cast easily into movable type, which helped the development of the [[Printing press|printing press]]. In 2022 global production was about 12 million tonnes, about two-thirds from recycling. Lead's high density, low melting point and resistance to oxidation made it useful in construction, plumbing, batteries, bullets, solder and radiation shielding. It is a neurotoxin that accumulates in soft tissues and bones and damages the [[Nervous system|nervous system]]. Its toxicity was noted by ancient Greek and Roman writers but widely recognized in Europe only in the late 19th century.

Principal appendage of the stem of a vascular plant, specialized for [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]. Leaves are usually flattened and borne laterally above ground, and collectively they form a plant's foliage. Most leaves are green because of [[Chlorophyll|chlorophyll]], which absorbs light energy from the [[Sun]]. The leaf draws water through xylem in the transpiration stream and takes in carbon dioxide through openings called [[Stoma|stomata]]. Sugars made in the leaf are stored as [[Starch|starch]] or converted into proteins and [[Cellulose|cellulose]]. Leaves vary widely in shape, size and texture. Broad leaves with complex veins, called megaphylls, occur in flowering plants and ferns, while some leaves, such as spines, have no major photosynthetic function. Modified leaves can serve as tendrils, spines or traps in [[Carnivorous plant|carnivorous plants]].

Plant-feeding insect of the family Cicadellidae, the second-largest family in the order [[Hemiptera]]. Leafhoppers suck sap from grasses, shrubs and trees using piercing mouthparts. Their hind legs are modified for jumping, and fine hairs spread a water-repellent secretion that also carries pheromones. They develop from nymph to adult without a [[Pupa|pupal]] stage. Most are drab, but some are colorful, and some have largely translucent wings. At least 20,000 species have been described. Many are pests or vectors of plant viruses and phytoplasmas. The beet leafhopper, for example, transmits beet curly top virus to tomato, tobacco and eggplant, and it is a serious vector in [[Chili pepper|chili pepper]] crops in the southwestern United States. Some species also eat small insects such as [[Aphid|aphids]].

Annual professional [[Esports|esports]] tournament for [[League of Legends]]. Hosted by Riot Games, it is the culmination of each season. Teams compete for the Summoner's Cup, a 22-pound (10-kilogram) trophy, and a multimillion-dollar prize. The 2018 final was watched by 99.6 million people, and the event is considered the most watched esports event in the world. Venues rotate among major countries and regions; the 2027 edition is set for [[Japan]] and [[South Korea]]. South Korea's T1 is the most successful team in the tournament's history, with six world championships.

Multiplayer online battle arena video game developed and published by Riot Games. Free-to-play since its October 2009 release, it is available for [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]] and [[MacOS|macOS]]. Two teams of five players battle on Summoner's Rift, each player controlling a character called a *champion*. Teams win by destroying the enemy's Nexus. In 2019 the game regularly peaked at 8 million concurrent players, and tie-ins include the animated series *Arcane*. It is the world's largest esport, and the [[League of Legends World Championship]] drew over 100 million unique viewers in 2019.

First worldwide intergovernmental organization, founded in 1920 to maintain world peace. Its Covenant formed part of the Treaty of Versailles after [[World War I]]. Its goals included collective security, disarmament and the arbitration of disputes. It lacked its own army and depended on the Allied powers to enforce its decisions. The United States never joined, and the League reached 58 members from September 1934 to February 1935. Japan and Germany left in 1933, Italy in 1937 and Spain in 1939. The [[Soviet Union]] joined in 1934 and was expelled in 1939 after invading Finland. Scholars generally agree that the League failed to prevent World War II but advanced collective security and raised awareness of epidemics, slavery and child labor. The [[United Nations]] replaced it in 1945 and inherited several of its agencies.

Freestanding bell tower of Pisa Cathedral, Italy. The tower is known for its lean of nearly four degrees, caused by an unstable foundation on soft ground. Construction began in 1173 and proceeded in three stages over 199 years. The tilt reached 5.5 degrees by 1990; remedial work from 1993 to 2001 reduced it to 3.97 degrees. The tower is 56.67 m tall on its high side and 55.86 m on its low side, and it weighs an estimated 14,500 tonnes. Part of the Piazza del Duomo, a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]], it receives over 5 million visitors a year. It is legendarily associated with [[Galileo Galilei]]'s experiments on falling bodies.

Intermittent one-second adjustment to [[Coordinated Universal Time|Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)]]. Between 1972 and 2016, 27 positive leap seconds were added to keep UTC within ±0.9 seconds of solar time, which varies as Earth's rotation slows. The last was on December 31, 2016, and since January 2017 the difference between UTC and [[Atomic clock|International Atomic Time]] has been 37 seconds. Their irregularity caused anomalies in some computing and satellite systems. On October 15, 2026, the General Conference on Weights and Measures voted to raise the permitted difference between UT1 and UTC to 3,600 seconds (one hour), effective May 20, 2027, deferring leap-second decisions for several centuries.

Calendar year containing an added day, or in lunisolar calendars an added month. The solar year lasts slightly less than 365¼ days, so calendars need extra time to stay aligned with the seasons. [[Julius Caesar]] reformed the Roman calendar in 45 BC, adding a leap day every 4 years to create the [[Julian calendar]]. The [[Gregorian calendar]], introduced in 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII, refined the rule: years divisible by 100 are leap years only if also divisible by 400, so 2000 was a leap year but 1900 was not. Lunisolar calendars, traditional across much of Asia, add a leap month instead. The term probably comes from the way a fixed date skips a weekday, advancing two days rather than one, in the year after a leap day. From 1972 to 2016, [[Leap second|leap seconds]] were also added to UTC.

Brain condition that makes it difficult to comprehend or process information. A learning disability is an official clinical diagnosis made by a professional such as a psychologist, while a learning disorder describes significant learning problems that may not meet diagnostic criteria. In the United Kingdom, the term generally refers to [[Intellectual disability|intellectual disability]], while conditions such as [[Dyslexia|dyslexia]] are called learning difficulties. Learning disorders include difficulties with reading (dyslexia), arithmetic ([[Dyscalculia|dyscalculia]]) and writing (dysgraphia). Interventions such as specialized instruction and technology help people build strategies, and a multidisciplinary team often designs them. Under the DSM-5, a specific learning disorder must persist for at least six months and cannot be explained by intellectual disability, sensory impairments or inadequate education.

Method of finding a best-fit model by minimizing the sum of squared residuals, the differences between observed and predicted values. The linear, or ordinary, problem has a closed-form solution and is central to [[Regression analysis|regression analysis]]; nonlinear problems are usually solved by iterative refinement. Its ideas developed during the 18th century, and [[Adrien-Marie Legendre]] published the method in 1805. [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] later gave it a probabilistic justification in 1809, assuming normally distributed errors. For normal, exponential, Poisson and binomial distributions, least-squares and maximum-likelihood estimates are identical.

Strong, flexible and durable material made by tanning animal skins and hides. It is most often made from cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, ostriches and aquatic animals such as seals and alligators. Tanning stabilizes the collagen in raw hide, so that the leather dries flexible and does not putrefy when rewetted. Preparatory stages such as soaking, liming and [[Pickling|pickling]] come before tanning, and crusting and finishing follow. Vegetable tanning, which uses [[Tannin|tannins]] from tree bark, is the oldest known method, while [[Chromium|chromium]] salts dominate modern output. Leather has been made for more than 7,000 years, and China and India are the leading producers today. Critics argue that tanneries engage in unsustainable practices that pose health hazards to nearby people and the environment.

Poetry collection by American poet [[Walt Whitman]]. Whitman self-published the first edition, which contained 12 untitled poems, on July 4, 1855, and he kept revising and expanding the book for the rest of his life. Later editions grew to more than 400 poems. The collection celebrates nature, the body and American democracy, and most of its poems do not rhyme or follow conventional meter. Its frank treatment of sensual pleasure provoked controversy and derision from contemporary critics, but it later became one of the central works of American poetry. The collection had its beginnings in [[Ralph Waldo Emerson]]'s essay "The Poet," which called for an American poet. Later editions added "When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd," an elegy for [[Abraham Lincoln]].

Multifaceted armed conflict in Lebanon, 1975–1990. It arose from tensions within Lebanon's sectarian political system, compounded by Palestinian armed groups and regional rivalries. Fighting began between Christian militias and Palestinian factions, principally the [[Palestine Liberation Organization]], and it later involved [[Syria]], [[Israel]] and [[Iran]] in shifting alliances. An estimated 120,000 people died, and nearly one million were displaced. The 1989 Taif Agreement laid the foundation for ending the war, and most militias disbanded after 1990. [[Hezbollah]] remained armed, citing its role in resisting the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon.

Country in the Levant region of West Asia. Officially the Lebanese Republic, it is bordered by [[Syria]] to the north and east, [[Israel]] to the south, and the Mediterranean Sea to the west. Its capital and largest city is [[Beirut]]. It was part of [[Phoenicia]] and later came under Roman, Arab and [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] rule. After World War I a French mandate created Greater Lebanon, and the country gained independence in 1943 under a confessional system that allocates offices by religious group. The [[Lebanese Civil War]] (1975–1990) was followed by Syrian occupation until 2005. The [[2020 Beirut explosion]] and a liquidity crisis precipitated the collapse of the currency, which the World Bank has described as one of the world's worst economic crises since the 19th century.

Polish statesman and anti-communist dissident, president of Poland from 1990 to 1995. An electrician at the Lenin Shipyard in [[Gdańsk]], he became a trade-union activist, was fired in 1976 and arrested several times. He helped negotiate the 1980 Gdańsk Agreement and co-founded the Solidarity trade union, whose membership rose to more than 10 million. After martial law outlawed Solidarity, he helped establish the Round Table Agreement, which led to the semi-free 1989 election. He was the first democratically elected president of Poland since 1922, but he narrowly lost the 1995 election. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983; his wife accepted it because he feared he would not be allowed to return to Poland. Documents from Poland's Institute of National Remembrance have been cited in claims that he was a paid informant for the communist secret police; he has called them fabrications.

Fourth studio album by [[Led Zeppelin]], released in 1971. The album was untitled and represented by four symbols, one for each band member. Atlantic Records released it on November 8, 1971, and [[Jimmy Page]] produced it. It was recorded mostly at Headley Grange in England between December 1970 and February 1971. It includes the eight-minute "Stairway to Heaven," one of the band's best-known recordings, and guest singer Sandy Denny performs on "The Battle of Evermore." Critics have often ranked it among the greatest albums. It has sold over 37 million copies worldwide, making it Led Zeppelin's best-selling album.

English rock band formed in London in 1968. The band comprised vocalist Robert Plant, guitarist [[Jimmy Page]], bassist and keyboardist John Paul Jones and drummer John Bonham. Evolving from the Yardbirds, it combined heavy electric guitar with blues and folk elements, helping to establish hard rock and heavy metal. The band released eight studio albums in ten years, including *Led Zeppelin IV* (1971). It achieved eight consecutive UK number-one albums and six number-one albums on the US Billboard 200. The band disbanded after Bonham's death from alcoholism in 1980. Its surviving members have reunited only occasionally, including for the 2007 Ahmet Ertegun Tribute Concert. The [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] inducted the band in 1995, and Forbes ranked Led Zeppelin the best rock band of all time in 2025.
